授業概要
This series of seminars is designed to provide an introduction to Taiwan as a fascinating field for research from various disciplinary perspectives – from History and Anthropology to Economics, Sociology, Political Science and Comparative Education. Beginning with a survey of Taiwan’s history from the 17th century onwards, it introduces students to the highly politicized contemporary debates surrounding that history, and their relationship to the ongoing controversy over Taiwan’s identity and political status. This is followed by a second set of five lectures examining the politics and economics of post-war and contemporary Taiwan, including the origins of Taiwan’s developmental success, and relevant aspects of the crucial relationship with the Chinese mainland (as well as other external relationships). Finally, the course turns to issues of culture and identity, which again involve the Cross-Strait relationship, reviewing the evolution of the debate over the nature of Taiwan as a community and a political entity. By the end of the course, students will have a clear awareness of the contours of Taiwan’s recent past, as well as a sense of the nature and significance of the ongoing controversies over Taiwan’s future.

授業計画
The sessions:
Part I – History and Historiography (and the politics of portraying the local past):
1. Taiwanese history I: prehistory to 1895, and recent historiographical controversy over the commemoration of Taiwan’s early history
2. Taiwanese history II: the Japanese colonial period, 1895-1945
3. Taiwanese history III: the post-war period: Martial Law and democratization
4. Film viewing: City of Sadness (悲情城市) - a crucial document of Taiwan’s post-Martial Law transition.
(Due to COVID-19, I may have to prepare an alternative presentation for this week.)
Part II – Politics and Economics:
5. Taiwan and the ‘East Asian Miracle’ – post-war developmental strategy in comparative perspective, with a special focus on the role of education
6. Debating the social and economic origins of Taiwan’s political transition from the 1970s to the 1990s.
7. The economics and politics of Taiwan’s external relations - the China factor and beyond
8. Migration - outbound and inbound - its political, economic and social implications.
Part III – Culture and Identity
9. Language, education, culture and identity during the Martial Law era.
10. The ‘nativisation’ (bentuhua) movement from the 1980s onwards – origins and implications.
11. Popular culture and the ‘Japan Craze’ (ha Ri yundong) of the 1990s and after – its meaning and significance.
12. Culture, tourism and Cross-Straits relations
13. Is Taiwan Chinese? The domestic and international contours of an ongoing debate. (Possibly including discussion of Allen Chun’s 2017 book, Forget Chineseness)

授業の進め方
Each week, students will be set one or two key readings relating to the following week’s session. The session will begin with a short lecture (about 30-40 minutes) on the week’s topic by Prof. Vickers or an invited scholar. This will be followed by questions and discussion related to the lecture and the set reading(s).
テキスト
Students are encouraged to try to access and read some of the texts listed below (in the 参考書 list). In particular, Denny Roy (2003) is a good introduction to Taiwanese history. This is a book I have drawn on quite a lot in preparing my lectures.
I may share further readings online or by email during the term.

学習相談
試験／成績評価の方法等
Each student seeking credits from this course is required to produce a proposal for a piece of original research on a Taiwan-related theme. The proposal should be written as if for a postgraduate thesis (at either MA or doctoral level). Students will be assigned a tutor with whom they can meet to briefly discuss their ideas. The proposals may be written in English or Japanese. Proposals written in English should be 2,500 words long, while those written in Japanese should be 5000字. Each proposal should consist of:
- An introduction explaining the focus of the proposed research and its significance.
- A brief review of existing research relevant to the proposed topic, and an explanation of how this new project will critique or extend this.
- A discussion of the key research questions that this project will address.
- A discussion of the methods and/or sources that will be used to answer these questions, and of their strengths and limitations.
